conversation.task: This is a fictional, low-stakes paper-story rehearsal. A hobby club has twenty minutes, three blank panels, scrap paper, and pencils to draft one understandable three-panel story display. A teammate says the first draft is confusing and proposes putting twelve narration slogans in its small opening panel. You think that panel will be hard to read. One imagined participant says a fast verbal explanation leaves them behind and asks for a written example. The group can try either a familiar lost-and-found story or a journey-home story; both are reversible paper sketches. The known downside is that trying a second story uses five of the twenty minutes. There is no evidence about which story the group prefers. Nobody has proposed a process. Reply in English in no more than 250 words. Include a short welcoming opening, your response to the proposal and concern, a comparison of feasible approaches with one usable example, and a usable plan for this bounded session. Treat all advice as provisional for the fictional group to choose; do not execute anything.
conversation.response:
Welcome—there’s room to make a clear little story together. These are provisional suggestions for your group to choose.

The confusing draft deserves another look. Twelve slogans might explain intentions, but I suspect they would crowd the small opening panel. Could you keep the teammate’s wording on scrap paper and test one short caption instead? Please keep objections visible; the concern may involve the pictures or sequence, too.

A lost-and-found story offers a concrete problem and resolution; a journey-home story offers a clear destination but may need extra clues about location. Either could work. We don’t know the group’s preference. A second sketch costs five minutes, leaving less time to improve the display.

Here’s a written lost-and-found example to read at your own pace:
1. Empty pocket: “Where’s my key?”
2. Key beside a bench: “There it is!”
3. Key opens the door: “Home at last.”

Suggested session checklist:
- [ ] Minutes 0–3: Share the written example, allow quiet reading, then invite preferences and concerns. Choose a provisional story together; if divided, agree which to test first.
- [ ] Minutes 3–8: Sketch three panels; check that each shows a necessary step.
- [ ] At minute 8: Ask someone to interpret the sketch without a verbal explanation. Record confusion and dissent.
- [ ] Minutes 8–13: Revise, or—if the group chooses—spend five minutes trying the alternative.
- [ ] Minutes 13–20: Choose together, simplify captions, check readability, and finish. If time slips, simplify drawings before skipping the reading check.
